children: The dispute turns on Tata Sons’ distinctive corporate structure and the RBI’s duty to apply and explain its rules consistently

Ahead of the Tata Sons board meeting reported for 17 September, the dispute over the group’s regulatory status has acquired a legal dimension. Reports on 15 September said that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court so that it could be heard before any interim order was passed if Tata Sons challenged the regulator’s decision. A caveat is a routine procedural safeguard. It neither prevents a challenge nor prejudges its outcome. The filing followed the RBI’s reported rejection of Tata Sons’ application to surrender its core investment company registration.

Separately, two Tata Group executives were cited as saying that Tata Trusts may first ask Tata Sons to seek a review of, and clarification on, the RBI’s decision before pursuing legal action. That course is expected to be discussed at the 17 September board meeting.

The dispute now intersects with Tata’s succession. N. Chandrasekaran’s term ends in February 2027. Sir Dorabji Tata Trust has initiated the formation of the committee that will recommend his successor, although its composition has not been announced and the process reportedly awaits the participation of Sir Ratan Tata Trust. That successor may inherit a company still seeking to remain closely held, or one preparing for the disciplines of public-market accountability.
The Regulatory Principle

The RBI has a credible regulatory case. It placed Tata Sons in the upper layer of non-banking financial companies in September 2022 and required such entities to list within three years. That deadline expired in September 2025. After repaying its borrowings, Tata Sons applied on 28 March 2024 to surrender its certificate of registration and operate as an unregistered core investment company. The RBI has reportedly declined the application and advised the company to comply with the applicable framework.

Scale is central to the issue. Tata Sons reported standalone total assets of about Rs 2.01 lakh crore at 31 March 2026, more than twice the current Rs 1 lakh crore upper-layer threshold. It sits at the apex of businesses spanning financial services, aviation, technology, automobiles and other sectors. The regulatory treatment of an entity of such scale cannot be viewed merely as an internal corporate matter. The framework exists because institutions at the top of large financial and corporate structures can have consequences that extend beyond their immediate balance sheets.

Tata Sons’ position also deserves to be understood. Its audited accounts reported nil borrowings and nil total public funds at 31 March 2026. Those facts support its case that a holding company in that position should not necessarily face the full regulatory consequences attached to an upper-layer NBFC. The framework, however, recognises the difficulty of isolating funds moving through group structures.

An RBI amendment issued on 29 April and effective from 1 July 2026 added an explicit explanation that indirect receipt of public funds includes funds received through associates and group entities that have access to public funds. This was a sector-wide amendment and does not by itself establish that Tata Sons receives such funds. The substantive question is whether repayment of direct borrowings has sufficiently changed Tata Sons’ risk profile within a deeply interconnected group.
Should Tata Sons Be Treated Differently?

The debate is larger than the listing of one company. For more than a century, the Tata name has been associated with institutional values, trusteeship and corporate governance. Its influence has grown from the scale of its businesses and from the belief that the institution must be larger than the individuals who lead it. That history strengthens its right to be heard; it does not settle the regulatory question.
That history strengthens Tata Sons’ right to be heard. It does not settle the regulatory question"

The RBI is entitled to ask why an institution of Tata Sons’ scale and character should sit outside a framework designed for systemically significant entities. Tata Sons is equally entitled to argue that a debt-free holding company whose audited accounts report nil public funds does not fit the risk the framework was designed to contain.

Its application to surrender registration followed a route contemplated by the rules, although whether Tata Sons satisfied the applicable conditions remained for the RBI to decide. If Tata Sons believes the framework has been applied incorrectly, it may seek judicial review. The RBI is likewise entitled to protect its position through a caveat. What matters is whether the framework is applied consistently and proportionately to Tata Sons’ present finances, scale and group linkages.

Tata Sons is the apex holding company of a complex group. The Tata Trusts own about 66 per cent, while the Shapoorji Pallonji Group holds 18.37 per cent. Listing would have consequences for control, shareholder rights, valuation and the private constitution that has governed the group for decades.

The SP Group’s position is an important part of the equation. A well-executed listing, preceded by a serious effort to rebuild trust with existing shareholders, could create an avenue for an orderly exit and help resolve long-running differences. Public ownership would also expose Tata Sons to continuous examination by institutional shareholders, analysts and markets.

Listing and governance therefore have to be considered together. Tata Sons must show that its preferred course is consistent with the standards it has long upheld. The RBI, equally, must explain why the same regulatory principle fits an entity with Tata Sons’ unusual structure.
A New Constitution For Tata

Listing Tata Sons would bring the private constitution of the Tata group under public-company governance. The Tata Trusts’ influence goes beyond their roughly two-thirds ownership. Under the Articles, the two principal Trusts may jointly nominate one-third of the directors while the Tata Trusts together retain at least 40 per cent.

Board resolutions requiring a majority also need the affirmative vote of a majority of the Trust-nominated directors present. A five-member selection committee recommends the chairman; the Tata Sons board formally makes the appointment. These arrangements form part of a governance model built for a closely held company.

That architecture is already shaping the immediate response. Reports indicate that Noel Tata favours remaining private while Venu Srinivasan supports listing, a division that could complicate any resolution involving Tata Sons’ capital structure.

Listing would require Tata Sons to become a public company and revise private-company provisions incompatible with the free transferability of public-company shares. Special rights would not automatically disappear, but would face securities-law scrutiny and, under current rules, periodic shareholder approval.

Whether each provision survives unchanged would depend on the final Articles and the application of company and securities law. The Trusts would remain the controlling shareholder, but their authority would operate within a more transparent and contestable framework. That shift could complicate a governance model built around patient capital, even as it strengthens external accountability. Tata Sons would also have to retain the confidence of shareholders with no historical or emotional connection to the Tata name, who would judge it on capital allocation, governance, performance and returns.
Speculation about Ambani or Adani should be kept in proportion. No public evidence has emerged that Reliance Industries, the Adani Group or their promoters are seeking Tata Sons shares.

A listing would make minority shares tradeable, subject to securities-law disclosure and takeover rules and any applicable RBI requirements. That is different from taking control. With the Trusts retaining roughly two-thirds and an initial public offer potentially as low as 2.5 per cent under the rules for very large issuers, subject to prescribed conditions, a takeover is not a realistic immediate consequence.

What could change is that minority influence at the apex of Tata acquires a market price. The Shapoorji Pallonji Group’s stake could become easier to monetise, while new institutions could enter the shareholder register over time. Tata Sons could be bought into. It could not easily be bought.
The Governance Test

The next chairman may inherit a complicated mandate: managing the Trusts, minority shareholders and the RBI, perhaps under public-market scrutiny, while preserving Tata’s long-term character. The task will be to reconcile trusteeship with public-company obligations and let the governance model evolve without losing what makes it distinctive.

The RBI’s reported decision will be read as a precedent beyond Tata Sons. Large institutions often argue that their complexity, ownership or strategic importance warrant different treatment; regulators must respond with consistent, proportionate and reasoned decisions. Tata Sons’ application remained pending while the framework evolved, including through the later explanation on indirect public funds. The decision should make clear which provisions apply and how.

Tata Sons should make its case on law, evidence and present risk, not reputation. If the framework is ultimately held to apply, compliance need not repudiate the Tata model; it could show that greater disclosure need not cost the group its long-term character.

The RBI need not choose Tata’s chairman or determine the group’s future. It must explain why Tata Sons’ balance sheet, scale and linkages place it within the framework; Tata Sons must show why they justify different treatment. The principle should be clear enough to govern the next comparable institution.
Noor Fathima Warsia
